planting.note: Direct sow in fall just ahead of winter rains, or set out small container plants on open, rocky upland bajada ground in full sun with no amendment to the native gravelly soil.

directions: Triangle-leaf bursage is the low, rounded gray-green subshrub that carpets the open ground between saguaro, foothill palo verde, and barrel cactus across classic Sonoran Desert bajada slopes, and it is the single most important nurse plant for saguaro seedlings, which germinate and hide beneath its canopy for their first vulnerable years. Its small triangular, felted leaves drop during severe drought to conserve moisture and flush back after rain, and inconspicuous greenish flower heads appear mainly in late winter and spring. It needs no irrigation once established in native rocky or gravelly bajada soil and resents any extra summer water or rich soil, which encourage rot and rank, floppy growth. Leave plenty of open space around each plant to mimic the spaced-out pattern it keeps naturally among desert shrubs and cacti.
sources: USDA Forest Service Fire Effects Information System

planting.note: Direct sow in fall on open, sun-baked bajada soil, or transplant small container stock into lean, rocky ground with no supplemental fertility; this species tolerates colder winters than most Sonoran bajada natives.

directions: White bursage is a compact, finely divided gray shrub whose pale, densely hairy foliage gives upland bajada and desert pavement ground a whitish cast, and it often co-dominates open bajada flats alongside triangle-leaf bursage and creosote bush, filling the spaces between the larger cacti and legume trees. Tiny greenish flower heads open in late winter and are wind-pollinated rather than showy, followed by small spiny burs that cling to passing animals. It is among the most drought-tolerant Sonoran natives, surviving on rainfall alone once rooted in and declining quickly if given regular irrigation or heavy soil. Give it full sun and sharp drainage and leave it unpruned, since its naturally rounded, twiggy form needs no shaping.
sources: USDA Forest Service Fire Effects Information System

planting.note: Sow seed on gritty, sterile cactus mix indoors in late winter, or set out small nursery-grown plants in spring tucked at the base of a bajada shrub where it gets a little afternoon shade and protection.

directions: Fishhook pincushion cactus is a small, solitary or loosely clustering globe cactus that hides low among the rocks and nurse shrubs of Sonoran Desert bajadas, its stout central spine curved into a distinctive hook. Pink to lavender funnel-shaped flowers ring the crown after summer monsoon rains, and the resulting club-shaped red fruits are unusual for taking until the following spring to fully ripen, often persisting on the plant through winter. It is easiest to establish from small nursery-grown plants set in extremely well-drained rocky or gravelly soil, siting it where it gets brief relief from the harshest afternoon sun as it would under natural bajada shrub cover. Keep it nearly dry outside of the summer rainy season, since excess water at any other time of year is the most common cause of rot.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

planting.note: Set out small nursery-grown clumps in spring on open, rocky bajada slopes in full sun with fast-draining, mineral soil; established clusters can also be divided by separating rooted offsets.

directions: Arizona hedgehog cactus forms loose mounding clusters of ribbed, spine-covered stems typical of rocky upland bajada slopes across the Sonoran Desert, often growing in the thin gravel between larger barrel cacti and palo verde trees. Large, brilliantly magenta-pink funnel flowers open in mid-spring and are followed by spiny, edible fruit that ripens in early summer. It establishes most reliably from nursery-grown clumps or divided offsets rather than slow-to-mature seed, and it needs essentially no irrigation once rooted into sharply drained rocky or decomposed granite soil. Avoid any soil that holds moisture, since stem rot rather than drought is the main threat to this species in cultivation.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in late spring once nights are reliably warm, siting them in full sun on well-drained rocky bajada soil away from frost pockets, since this species is more cold-sensitive than the common cane ocotillo.

directions: Tree ocotillo is a close, more tree-like relative of the familiar cane ocotillo, native to the rocky foothills and bajada thornscrub of mainland Sonora, where it develops a short, thick, semi-succulent trunk that branches into a crown of spiny, gray-green stems rather than the single cluster of thin whip-like canes typical of Fouquieria splendens. Clusters of tubular orange-red flowers open at the branch tips mainly in spring and intermittently after warm-season rain, drawing hummingbirds. It is noticeably less cold-hardy than cane ocotillo and should be reserved for warmer low-desert bajada sites, protected from hard freezes while young. Give it full sun and sharply drained rocky soil and withhold irrigation once established, since wet feet in winter are far more damaging than summer drought.

planting.note: Set out small container plants in spring near the roots of an established palo verde, creosote, or bursage on open bajada ground, since this species is a partial root parasite and establishes most reliably with a host shrub nearby.

directions: White ratany is a stiff, intricately branched, gray-stemmed shrub scattered across open rocky bajada slopes, where its roots tap into the roots of nearby shrubs as a facultative hemiparasite, drawing some water and nutrients from its neighbors without seriously harming them. Small but striking magenta-purple flowers with fringed petals open in spring and are pollinated almost exclusively by specialized oil-collecting desert bees rather than typical nectar feeders. It is slow to establish and grows best when sited within a few feet of an existing palo verde, creosote, or bursage rather than planted in isolated open ground. Give it full sun, lean rocky soil, and minimal supplemental water, since this species is adapted to survive on rainfall alone even in the driest bajada microsites.
sources: USDA Forest Service Fire Effects Information System

planting.note: Direct sow onto open, bare bajada ground right at the start of summer monsoon rains, scattering seed over disturbed or gravelly soil that will stay briefly moist after storms.

directions: Arizona poppy is a sprawling, monsoon-triggered summer annual that can blanket open bajada slopes and roadside flats in bright orange, five-petaled, poppy-like flowers within days of the first good July or August rain. Its ferny, pinnately divided leaves fold flat at night and during intense heat, and plants complete their entire life cycle from germination to seed set within a single warm season before dying back at the first fall frost. It thrives on nothing more than seasonal monsoon rainfall and bare, disturbed, well-drained bajada soil, making supplemental irrigation unnecessary and even counterproductive to its natural boom-and-bust rhythm. Once established in a planting area it self-sows reliably, returning in good numbers after any summer with adequate monsoon moisture.
